Title: Passage 2: The Story of Books
Author: by Amy Tao
Content: Before there were books, people learned stories by heart and taught new `text(ones)` to each other. Sometimes it was hard to remember them all.
Things grew a little easier when writing was invented.
The `text(first)` writers made marks by pressing sticks into slabs of soft clay. When baked, the clay became hard and strong.

At `text(first)`, the new marks were just used to make lists. But soon people were writing down laws, and then stories. Imagine if `text(each page)` of `text(one)` of your books were a clay block instead of a piece of paper.

The ancient Egyptians wrote their stories on flat sheets made from papyrus plants. They glued many papyrus sheets together to make `text(one)` long strip. Then they rolled the strip around a stick to make a scroll that could be tied shut with papyrus string.

People in other places learned to use papyrus from the Egyptians, but papyrus plants grew mainly in Egypt. So in colder places people used parchment instead, made from calfskin or goatskin stretched thin.
In Central and South America, long before the Europeans came, the Mayas and Aztecs had huge libraries filled with brightly colored books made from deerskin or papery bark.
In ancient China, books looked a little different. People there `text(first)` carved words into bone or tortoise shell. Later they used ink to write on strips of bamboo or silk.
Then the Chinese invented paper. Made from a watery mush of tree bark and old rags, paper was cheap and easy to make. Its surface was smoother and better for writing on than papyrus or parchment.

Every `text(single)` book had to be copied out by hand. If there were pictures, `text(each page)` had to be painted by hand, `text(one)` at a time. This made books rare and expensive though also very beautiful.

The Chinese were the `text(first)` to think of a way to speed things up a little. They carved a page of words and pictures into a block of wood or stone. Then they printed the entire page at `text(once)` by spreading ink on the block and pressing it against paper. This let them make many copies of a book much more quickly.

Then a German named Johannes Gutenberg invented movable, metal letters. A person could set metal letters in a tray to spell out any words she wanted. The tray of letters could be used to print copy after copy, and then the letters could be rearranged again and again to print different pages of words. What a time saver!
`text(Once)`, books were a luxury only the rich could buy. But with the printing press, they soon became a treasure everyone could enjoy.
